title: Ibn Khaldun
hook: the historian of Tunis who studied how societies rise and fall

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ibn Battuta, who set out from Tangier for Mecca and kept going. Your line was: the traveler.

Damascus is under siege. Outside the walls is the army of Timur, the conqueror. Inside, a scholar from North Africa decides he wants to meet the man himself. The gates are closed, so his friends lower him down the city wall on ropes. He walks into the conqueror's camp, is received, and the two talk about history, about kings, about the lands of the west. The scholar tells this himself, in the account of his own life. He was Ibn Khaldun, born in Tunis, and he had spent years thinking about exactly this: why some peoples rise and conquer, and why their cities, in time, fall.
screen: `DAMASCUS UNDER SIEGE.` → `LOWERED DOWN THE WALL ON ROPES.` → `A SCHOLAR MEETS A CONQUEROR.`

segments.voice: Ibn Khaldun served sultans across North Africa and al-Andalus, fell in and out of favor, spent time in prison, and finally withdrew to a quiet fortress to write. He began with an introduction to a history of the world, and the introduction took on a life of its own: the Muqaddimah, the introduction. His big idea has an Arabic name, asabiyya. Group feeling: the bond that holds a people together, the loyalty that makes them stand by each other. He saw it strongest among people living hard lives in the desert and the mountains, where nobody survives alone. That bond, he argued, lets a group win power and build a state. Then comes the city. Comfort: fine clothes, soft beds, servants. Each generation inherits the power without the hardship that made it, and the bond quietly loosens. Rulers lean on paid soldiers instead of loyal kin. And one day a new group, with strong bonds and nothing to lose, comes in from the edge. He was writing about dynasties, but the question travels: anyone can ask it of a family, a team or a mosque community. The Qur'an has a line some readers set beside his idea. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! Allah changeth not the condition of a folk until they (first) change that which is in their hearts." Ibn Khaldun wrote as a believing Muslim and a judge. For him, studying how societies rise and fall was a way of reading the world with open eyes. Bonds build, luxury loosens.
screen: `A JUDGE WITHDRAWS TO WRITE.` · `ASABIYYA — GROUP FEELING.` · `HARDSHIP BINDS, COMFORT LOOSENS.` · `A NEW GROUP COMES IN FROM THE EDGE.` · then, large: `BONDS BUILD, LUXURY LOOSENS.`

segments.voice: Pick one group you belong to, a family, friends, a congregation, a team at work, and ask Ibn Khaldun's question gently: what holds it together, and where has comfort or busyness let the bond loosen a little? Don't blame anyone; just notice, and think of one person in it you've drifted from. If you pray, hold that group before God; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.
Ibn Khaldun. The scholar born in Tunis whose Muqaddimah asks how group feeling builds a state, and how comfort loosens it. Today's word.
Your line: bonds build, luxury loosens. Comfort is a gift worth watching. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah is read today by historians, sociologists and students of Islamic thought, and its idea of asabiyya, group feeling, is still discussed.

chat.says: What did Ibn Khaldun think makes a group rise and then fall?
options: A strong bond, asabiyya, builds power; then comfort loosens it, and a new group rises.
Only the size of its army: the biggest army always wins, and bonds don't matter.
Comfort makes the bond stronger, so a dynasty lasts as long as it stays rich.
chat.meaning: In the Muqaddimah, asabiyya, group feeling, lets a group win power; later generations inherit it without the hardship, and the bond loosens.
